questions.q: Why is AUTO_CLOSE generally left off in production?
options: It shuts the database down between connections, cold-starting it on the next connection and fighting connection pooling
It permanently deletes the transaction log
It disables all indexes on the database
It is required to be off before you can create a backup
questions.explain: AUTO_CLOSE releases the database's resources when the last connection closes and reopens it on the next one — a cold-start cost that conflicts with connection pooling's assumption that a database stays warm.

questions.q: Why is AUTO_SHRINK considered a real anti-pattern?
options: Shrinking compacts the file by moving pages, causing serious index fragmentation, and the space often just grows back
It has no effect on the database at all
It only works on the transaction log, never data files
It is only available in SQL Server Express
questions.explain: AUTO_SHRINK periodically shrinks files automatically, which fragments indexes badly, and the file frequently grows back on the next load — so you pay the fragmentation cost with no lasting benefit.

questions.q: What does READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON actually change?
options: READ COMMITTED starts using row versioning instead of locking, so readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking behind writer locks
It changes the database's recovery model to SIMPLE
It disables all transaction logging
It forces every query to run at SERIALIZABLE isolation
questions.explain: READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT switches the default READ COMMITTED isolation level to use row versioning, eliminating a large class of reader/writer blocking at the cost of tempdb version-store overhead.

questions.q: What must be true of the database's connections before setting READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON?
options: There must be no other active connections — it's set WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE
The database must be in SIMPLE recovery model
AUTO_SHRINK must be enabled first
The database must be offline permanently
questions.explain: READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT requires exclusive access to change; ALTER DATABASE ... SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE rolls back other active transactions to apply it.

questions.q: What does PAGE_VERIFY CHECKSUM do, and why should it almost always be on?
options: It writes and verifies a checksum on every page I/O to detect storage-layer corruption; it's been the default since SQL Server 2005
It checks T-SQL syntax before execution
It verifies login credentials on every connection
It only applies to tempdb, not user databases
questions.explain: CHECKSUM computes and stores a checksum for every page on write and verifies it on read, catching torn pages and most corruption — there's essentially never a reason to use TORN_PAGE_DETECTION or NONE instead.
